dialogues.title: Dialogue 1
dialogues.setting: Mr Chan finds out how his colleague Miss Cheung spends her time off

lines.speaker: Mr Chan
lines.zh: 张小姐，昨日同前日都放假。你有冇去打波呀？
lines.jp: zoeng1 siu2 ze2, zok6 jat6 tung4 cin4 jat6 dou1 fong3 gaa3. nei5 jau5 mou5 heoi3 daa2 bo1 aa3?
lines.en: Miss Cheung, you take times off for the past two days, did you go play a ball game?

lines.speaker: Miss Cheung
lines.jp: ngo5 m4 zung1 ji3 daa2 bo1 ge3
lines.en: I don't like playing ball games

lines.speaker: Mr Chan
lines.jp: jau5 mou5 heoi3 kei4 taa1 dei6 fong1 waan2 ne1?
lines.en: Did you go to other places?

lines.speaker: Miss Cheung
lines.zh: 我都唔中意离开香港嘅，我只係中意睇电影啫。
lines.jp: ngo5 dou1 m4 zung1 ji3 lei4 hoi1 hoeng1 gong2 ge3, ngo5 zi2 hai6 zung1 ji3 tai2 din6 jing2 ze1
lines.en: I don't like leaving Hong Kong. I only like watching movies

lines.speaker: Mr Chan
lines.zh: 我知道昨日喺大会堂有一出好有名嘅电影。你有冇去睇呀？
lines.jp: ngo5 zi1 dou6 zok6 jat6 hai2 daai6 wui6 tong4 jau5 jat1 ceot1 hou2 jau5 meng2 ge3 din6 jing2. nei5 jau5 mou5 heoi3 tai2 aa3?
lines.en: I know yesterday there was a famous movie at the city hall. Did you go watch it?

lines.speaker: Miss Cheung
lines.zh: 有呀！真係好好睇呀。而且仲好刺激添。
lines.jp: jau5 aa3! zan1 hai6 hou2 hou2 tai2 aa3. ji4 ce2 zung6 hou2 ci3 gik1 tim1
lines.en: Yes! It was really good. And it was also very exciting!

lines.speaker: Mr Chan
lines.zh: 刺激！我唔觉得啵。你记唔记得嗰出电影嘅内容呀？
lines.jp: ci3 gik1! ngo5 m4 gok3 dak1 bo3. nei5 gei3 m4 gei3 dak1 go2 ceot1 din6 jing2 ge3 noi6 jung4 aa3?
lines.en: Exciting! I don't feel that way. Do you remember the content of the movie?

lines.speaker: Miss Cheung
lines.zh: 对唔住，我一啲都唔记得勒，因为我同男朋友一齐去睇嘅。
lines.jp: deoi3 m4 zyu6, ngo5 jat1 di1 dou1 m4 gei3 dak1 laak3, jan1 wai4 ngo5 tung4 naam4 pang4 jau5 jat1 cai4 heoi3 tai2 ge3
lines.en: Sorry, I don't remember any bit, because I went to watch it with my boyfriend

dialogues.title: Dialogue 2
dialogues.setting: Mr Wong and Mr Cheung discuss keeping fit, but Mr Wong is not sure that the theories apply to his wife!

lines.speaker: Mr Wong
lines.zh: 张先生，你话时时运动可以减少身体里便多余嘅脂肪，对健康好好，係唔係呀？
lines.jp: zoeng1 sin1 saang1, nei5 waa6 si4 si4 wan6 dung6 ho2 ji5 gaam2 siu2 san1 tai2 leoi5 bin6 do1 jyu4 ge3 zi1 fong1, deoi3 gin6 hong1 hou2 hou2, hai6 m4 hai6 aa3?
lines.en: Mr Cheung, you said exercise frequently can reduce the surplus fats in the body, it's good for health, is it right?

lines.speaker: Mr Cheung
lines.zh: 係呀！我时时都行路，爬山，同打波。你睇我已经五十几岁勒，仲係好健康，好似四十几岁咁上下。
lines.jp: hai6 aa3! ngo5 si4 si4 dou1 haang4 lou6, paa4 saan1, tung4 daa2 bo1. nei5 tai2 ngo5 ji5 ging1 ng5 sap6 gei2 seoi3 laak3, zung6 hai6 hou2 gin6 hong1, hou2 ci5 sei3 sap6 gei2 seoi3 gam3 soeng6 haa2
lines.en: Right! I walk, climb mountains, and play balls frequently. I am already 50 something, but I'm still very healthy, I only look like I'm in my 40s

lines.speaker: Mr Wong
lines.zh: 但係我觉得健康对我太太一啲用都冇。
lines.jp: daan6 hai6 ngo5 gok3 dak1 gin6 hong1 deoi3 ngo5 taai3 taai3 jat1 di1 jung6 dou1 mou5
lines.en: But I think health has no use for my wife

lines.speaker: Mr Cheung
lines.zh: 一定有用嘅。只要你太太时时运动，身体里便一定冇多余脂肪嘅。
lines.jp: jat1 ding6 jau5 jung6 ge3. zi2 jiu3 nei5 taai3 taai2 si4 si4 wan6 dung6, san1 tai2 leoi5 bin6 jat1 ding6 mou5 do1 jyu4 zi1 fong1 ge3
lines.en: It must have some kind of use. If your wife often exercises, her body should have no surplus fats

lines.speaker: Mr Wong
lines.zh: 我太太成日讲嘢，口部嘅肌肉有好多运动喇。点解佢仲有一个好多脂肪嘅双下巴呢？
lines.jp: ngo5 taai3 taai2 sing4 jat6 gong2 je5, hau2 bou6 ge3 gei1 juk6 jau5 hou2 do1 wan6 dung6 laa1. dim2 gaai2 keoi5 zung6 jau5 jat1 go3 hou2 do1 zi1 fong1 ge3 soeng1 haa6 paa4 ne1?
lines.en: My wife talks the whole day, she exercises her mouth muscle frequently, how come she still has a double chin with lots of fats?

grammar.title: fong3 gaa3 to have a holiday
grammar.summary: fong3 gaa3 (lit. to release a day off) is a verb-object expression, and such expressions can be split up if the sense allows.
grammar.body: fong3 gaa3 literally means to release a day off. It is one of a quite a large group of expressions which are made up of a verb and an object and these expressions can all be split up if the sense allows. Here are a couple of examples:

examples.jp: ngo5 ni1 go3 sing1 kei4 fong3 saam1 jat6 gaa3
examples.en: I have three days' holiday this week

examples.jp: keoi5 zou6 zau2 lau4 ge3 saang1 ji3
examples.en: He is in the restaurant business

grammar.title: Playing ball
grammar.summary: bo1 comes from English 'ball' and daa2 means to hit, so daa2 bo1 is the regular way to say to play a ball game; tai2 daa2 bo1 is to watch the game.
grammar.body: The word bo1 originally came from the English word ball. Daa2 means to hit and daa2 bo1 is the regular way to say to play a ball game. The problem is Which ball game? For a majority of people it means soccer, but if you happen to be a football fan then it means football, or for a basketball fan it means basketball, and then of course there is table tennis, tennis…For the moment, daa2 bo1 is all you need, but you might note the very logical difference between the following:

examples.jp: ngo5 heoi3 daa2 bo1
examples.en: I'm going off to play ball

examples.jp: ngo5 heoi3 tai2 daa2 bo1
examples.en: I'm going off to watch the game

grammar.title: Going to the movies
grammar.summary: tai2 din6 jing2 is to see a film (a verb plus object expression); tai2 hei3 to see a play is now also commonly used for going to the pictures.
grammar.body:
Tai2 din6 jing2 means to see a film and heoi3 tai2 din6 jing2 is to go to the movies. You will notice that tai2 din6 jing2 is also a verb plus object expression. So another example for this might be:
There is another expression tai2 hei3, which means to see a play, but far more people go to the cinema than go to the live theatre and it is now very common to hear someone say ngo5 heoi3 tai2 hei3 when they mean I'm going to the pictures.

examples.jp: Wong4 taai2 soeng2 heoi3 tai2 mei5 gwok3 din6 jing2
examples.en: Mrs. Wong wants to go to see an American film

examples.jp: ngo5 heoi3 tai2 hei3

grammar.title: Taking shortcuts again
grammar.summary: Choice questions with a two-syllable verb can be shortened: nei5 gei3 m4 gei3 dak1 for nei5 gei3 dak1 m4 gei3 dak1.
grammar.body:
In Unit 3 we met the sentence nei5 faan1 m4 faan1 heoi3 aa3? and it was explained that this was a common shortened form of nei5 faan1 heoi3 m4 faan1 heoi3 aa3?
You can do the same thing with any two-syllable verb and in the dialogue you will have noticed nei5 gei3 m4 gei3 dak1 where Mr Chan might equally well correctly have said nei5 gei3 dak1 m4 gei3 dak1. Here is another example:

examples.jp: nei5 faan1 m4 faan1 heoi3 aa3?
nei5 faan1 heoi3 m4 faan1 heoi3 aa3?
nei5 gei3 m4 gei3 dak1
nei5 gei3 dak1 m4 gei3 dak1
nei5 zung1 m4 zung1 ji3 leon4 deon1 aa3?

grammar.title: Not even a little bit!
grammar.summary: jat1 di1 a little bit combined with dou1 and the negatives m4 or mou5 means not even a little bit.
grammar.body:
Jat1 di1 means a little bit and combined with dou1 and the negatives m4 or mou5 it means not even a little bit.
Along the same line, you can also say ngo5 dei6 jat1 di1 cin2 dou1 mou5 (can you guess the meaning of this? This is something that lots of Cantonese people say all the time)

examples.jp: ngo5 dei6 jat1 di1 cin2 dou1 mou5
examples.en: We haven't got any money at all

examples.jp: ngo5 jat1 di1 dou1 m4 gei3 dak1 laak3

grammar.title: Deoi3 to face
grammar.summary: deoi3 means to face; from it come towards, regarding / with regard to, a pair (classifier for chopsticks) and, in Guangzhou, correct (Hong Kong uses ngaam1).
grammar.body:
Deoi3 means to face, and from this a number of other meanings and expressions derive. We have already met deoi3 m4 zyu6 (I face you but can't stand my ground) I'm sorry.
And if you face something you are looking towards it, so deoi3 also means towards and regarding, and from that it means with regard to, concerning.
Things which face each other and match make a pair, and deoi3 means a pair too, so it is the classifier for chopsticks.
And from there an answer which matches a question is also deoi3 correct (or at least it is in Guangzhou, but Hong Kong people tend to use another word for correct – ngaam1).

examples.jp: deoi3 m4 zyu6
examples.lit: I face you but can't stand my ground

examples.jp: gin6 hong1 deoi3 ngo5 taai3 taai3 jat1 di1 jung6 dou1 mou5
examples.en: Health has no use for my wife (Dialogue 2)

grammar.title: gei2 several
grammar.summary: gei2 means how many? but also several, often combined with numbers (ji6 sap6 gei2 twenty-odd, gei2 sap6 several tens).
grammar.body:
We met gei2 in the expression gei2 do1? how many? in Unit 5 and gei2 si4? when? in Unit 8. On its own gei2 can also mean how many?, but it has the meaning several as well, and that could be quite confusing.
Supposing someone were to say to you gei2 go3 jan4, you couldn't be sure whether they were saying how many people? or several people. Obviously the context in which they said it would help a lot, but in practice if it were a question most people would add aa3? on the end and that would of course make it clear.
In its several meaning, gei2 gets involved with numbers quite a lot.

examples.jp: gei2 go3 jan4
ji6 sap6 gei2 go3 jan4
examples.en: More than 20 people (i.e. more than 20 but fewer than 30)

examples.jp: sap6 gei2 seoi3 ge3 zung1 gwok3 jan4
gei2 sap6 go3 jan4
examples.en: Dozens of people (several tens of people)

examples.jp: gei2 sap6 nin4

grammar.title: seoi3 years of age
grammar.summary: seoi3 takes no classifier (like jat6 and nin4) and is often used without a verb; if a verb is used it is usually hai6.
grammar.body:
There are two points to be noted about seoi3.
First, it is one of those few words which (like jat6 and nin4) do not need a classifier.
Second, it is often used without a verb. If you want to or feel the need to put in a verb, the most commonly used one is hai6 to be. Mr Cheung could have said: ngo5 ji5 ging1 hai6 ng5 sap6 gei2 seoi3 laak3 and it would have meant the same

examples.jp: ngo5 ji5 ging1 ng5 sap6 gei2 seoi3 laak3
ngo5 ji5 ging1 hai6 ng5 sap6 gei2 seoi3 laak3

grammar.title: Approximately
grammar.summary: gam3 soeng5 haa2 (lit. thus up and down) means approximately and usually follows whatever it refers to.
grammar.body:
Gam3 soeng5 haa2 literally means thus up and down and from that comes to mean approximately.
It usually follows whatever it refers to, as it does where you met it in the dialogue: ng5 sap6 gei2 seoi3 gam3 soeng5 haa2

examples.jp: gam3 soeng5 haa2
ng5 sap6 gei2 seoi3 gam3 soeng5 haa2

grammar.title: sing4 the whole
grammar.summary: sing4- combines with classifiers to make the whole….
grammar.body: Sing4- combines with classifiers to make the whole…

examples.jp: sing4 go3 lai5 baai3
sing4 jat6
examples.en: The whole day, all day long

examples.jp: sing4 nin4

grammar.title: Another lonely verb
grammar.summary: gong2 is a 'lonely' verb that needs an object; je5 things is handy as the supplied object (gong2 je5, sik6 je5, maai5 je5, jam2 je5).
grammar.body:
In Mr Wong's last speech, he says ngo5 taai3 taai2 sing4 jat6 gong2 je5. Je5 means things, as we learned in Unit 8, but here it is merely doing duty as the supplied object for the verb gong2 which is one of those which gets lonely on its own.
Je5 is quite handy for this purpose: here are a few more examples of it with lonely verbs:

examples.jp: ngo5 taai3 taai2 sing4 jat6 gong2 je5
examples.en: My wife talks the whole day (Dialogue 2)

examples.jp: nei5 soeng2 m4 soeng2 sik6 je5?
ngo5 taai3 taai2 heoi3 zo2 maai5 je5
keoi5 sing4 jat6 dou1 jam2 je5

grammar.title: Negation
grammar.summary: Cantonese negative words all begin with the nasal m and have low-register tones: m4, mou5, mei6, m4 hai6 and the prefix m-.
grammar.body:
To express negation, Cantonese uses negative words that all begin with the nasal consonant m and have low-register tones:
m4 not – used with adjectives, verbs referring to the present
mou5 have not – used with nouns, verbs referring to the past
mei6 not yet – used with verbs
m4 hai6 is not – used with sentences
m- un- – antonyms of adjectives and verbs

examples.jp: m4
examples.en: Not (adjectives, verbs referring to the present)

examples.jp: mou5
examples.en: Have not (nouns, verbs referring to the past)

examples.jp: mei6
m4 hai6
m4
examples.en: Un- (as the prefix m-: antonyms of adjectives and verbs)

grammar.title: m4 is used to negate
grammar.summary: m4 negates most adjectives and verbs referring to the present.
grammar.body:
m4 is used to negate:
(i) most adjectives
(ii) verbs referring to the present:

examples.jp: ni1 gin6 saam1 m4 peng4 gaa3
di1 zi6 m4 cing1 co2
ngo5 ging1 jim6 m4 gau3
ngo5 gam1 jat6 m4 faan1 hok6
examples.en: I'm not going to school today

examples.jp: keoi5 dei6 m4 sau1 jin6 gam1
gung1 si1 zaam6 si4 m4 ceng2 jan4
examples.en: The company is not hiring anyone right now

grammar.title: mou5 is the negative form of jau5
grammar.summary: mou5 (negative of jau5) is used as a main verb (not have) and as an auxiliary, where it is the negative counterpart of zo2.
grammar.body:
Mou5 is the negative form of jau5, used in two main ways:
(i) as a main verb:
(ii) as an auxiliary verb:
Used in this way serves as the negative counterpart to zo2 as can be seen in pairs like the following:

examples.jp: keoi5 mou5 naam4 pang4 jau5 ge3
ngo5 dei6 ji4 gaa1 mou5 gung1 jan4
examples.en: We don't have a (domestic) helper now

examples.jp: ngo5 mou5 leng3 saam1 zeok3
examples.en: I have no nice clothes to wear

examples.jp: ngo5 gam1 jat6 mou5 gin3 dou2 keoi5 aa3
keoi5 mou5 lai4 hoi1 wui2
examples.en: He didn't come to the meeting

examples.jp: keoi5 dei6 mou5 tung1 zi1 ngo5 dei6
ngo5 kam4 jat6 maai5 zo2 coi3
ngo5 kam4 jat6 mou5 maai5 coi3
gung1 si1 ceng2 zo2 keoi5
gung1 si1 mou5 ceng2 keoi5
examples.en: The company has not hired him

grammar.title: mei6 not yet
grammar.summary: mei6 as an auxiliary means not yet; attached to the end of a statement it makes a special form of question, typically with zo2 or gwo3.
grammar.body:
Mei6 as an auxiliary has the meaning 'not yet'
Attached to the end of a statement, mei6 makes a special form of question, typically with zo2 or gwo3:

examples.jp: ngo5 dei6 zung6 mei6 bun1 nguk1
lou5 baan2 zung6 mei6 faan1 lai4
examples.en: The boss hasn't come in yet

examples.jp: zaam6 si4 mei6 jau5 siu1 sik1
examples.en: So far there hasn't been any news

examples.jp: nei5 zou6 zo2 gung1 fo3 mei6 aa3?
nei5 heoi3 gwo3 hoi2 joeng4 gung1 jyun2 mei6 aa3
examples.en: Have you ever been to Ocean Park?

grammar.title: m4 hai6 it's not
grammar.summary: m4 hai6 (mhai6) it's not is the negative of hai6 to be; it is used to negate adjectives modified by an adverb.
grammar.body: Mhai6 'it's not' is the negative form of the verb hai6 'to be'. It's used in negating adjectives modified by an adverb:

examples.jp: m4 hai6 hou2 leng3
m4 hai6 gei2 gung1 ping4
ngo5 dei6 m4 hai6 gam3 suk6
examples.en: We're not that familiar (with each other)

grammar.title: Antonyms formed with negation
grammar.summary: Adding the prefix m- forms antonyms of many adjectives and some verbs; some carry a related but not simply opposite meaning, and a few words are inherently negative.
grammar.body:
Antonyms of many adjectives (and some verbs) can be formed by adding a prefix m-:
Some of these negative forms carry a meaning related to that of the underlying verb or adjective but not simply its opposite:
Modified by hou2 or other adverbs:
A few words are inherently negative, without the prefix m-, they do not occur in an affirmative statement:

examples.jp: hoi1 sam1 —> m4 hoi1 sam1
cing1 co2 —> m4 cing1 co2
gung1 ping4 —> m4 gung1 ping4
tung4 ji3 —> m4 tung4 ji3
gin3 —> m4 gin3
gei3 dak1 —> m4 gei3 dak1
tung4 —> m4 tung4
dak1 haan4 —> m4 dak1 haan4
syu1 fuk6 —> m4 syu1 fuk6
keoi5 hou2 m4 zung1 ji3 ni1 go3 tai4 ji5
Gam2 joeng2 deoi3 ngo5 taai3 m4 gung1 ping4
examples.en: This is too unfair to me

examples.jp: m4 hou2 ji3 si1
m4 fan6 hei3
keoi5 gok3 dak1 hou2 m4 hou2 ji3 si1
ngo5 gok3 dak1 hou2 m4 fan6 hei3

grammar.title: Double negatives
grammar.summary: Two negatives combine to give a qualified or indirect positive: m4 hai6 denying a negative statement, or negating both an auxiliary and the main verb.
grammar.body:
Combinations of two negative forms are widely used to give a qualified or indirect positive meaning. A typical case is to use m4 hai6 to deny a negative statement:
Another case involves negating both the main verb and an auxiliary

examples.jp: ngo5 m4 hai6 m4 seon3 nei5
examples.en: It's not that I don't believe you

examples.jp: m4 hai6 m4 ho2 nang4 ge3
ngo5 dei6 m4 hai6 mou5 hei1 mong6
examples.en: We're not without hope (i.e. we still have a chance)

examples.jp: keoi5 m4 wui5 m4 faan1 lai4
examples.en: He won't fail to come back

examples.jp: Gam2 joeng2 m4 wui5 m4 gung1 ping4
nei5 m4 ho2 ji5 m4 bei2 cin2
examples.en: You cannot choose not to pay (i.e. you have to pay)

items.prompt: a. FS: Good morning, Mr Wong.
items.answer: zou2 san4, Wong4 sin1 saang1
items.hint: Mr Wong replies: 早晨 zou2 san4

items.prompt: b. FS: Would you like to have a beer?
items.answer: nei5 soeng2 m4 soeng2 jam2 be1 zau2 aa3?
items.answer_en: Would you like to drink beer?
items.hint: nei5 jiu3 m4 jiu3 jam2 be1 zau2 aa3? also works. Mr Wong replies: 我唔中意饮啤酒 ngo5 m4 zung1 ji3 jam2 be1 zau2 (I don't like drinking beer)

items.prompt: c. FS: Oh, well how about coffee? Or tea?
items.answer: gam2, gaa1 fe1 ne1? caa4 ne1?
items.answer_en: Well then, how about coffee? Tea?
items.hint: Several phrasings possible, e.g. nei5 jam2 m4 jam2 gaa1 fe1 aa3? Mr Wong replies: 咖啡同茶都对身体唔好。我只係饮水啫。gaa1 fe1 tung4 caa4 dou1 deoi3 san1 tai2 m4 hou2. ngo5 zi2 hai6 jam2 seoi2 ze1 (Coffee and tea are both bad for the body. I only drink water)

items.prompt: d. FS: I'm sorry, we have no water. My wife told me that the water here is not good to drink. Why don't you have some beer?
items.answer: deoi3 m4 zyu6, ngo5 dei6 mou5 seoi2. ngo5 taai3 taai2 waa6 ngo5 zi1 ni1 dou6 di1 seoi2 m4 hou2 jam2. nei5 jam2 di1 be1 zau2 laa1
items.answer_en: Sorry, we have no water. My wife told me the water here is not good to drink. Have some beer
items.hint: Free translation; check with tutor. Mr Wong replies: 你成日话我要饮啤酒。我已经话你知我唔中意饮。你真係好唔客气。nei5 sing4 jat6 waa6 ngo5 jiu3 jam2 be1 zau2. ngo5 ji5 ging1 waa6 nei5 zi1 ngo5 m4 zung1 ji3 jam2. nei5 zan1 hai6 hou2 m4 haak3 hei3 (You keep telling me to drink beer. I've already told you I don't like drinking it. You are really impolite)

items.prompt: e. FS: The beer is very good, it's British beer. Please drink a little.
items.answer: di1 be1 zau2 hou2 hou2, hai6 jing1 gwok3 be1 zau2. ceng2 nei5 jam2 jat1 di1 laa1
items.answer_en: The beer is very good, it's British beer. Please drink a little
items.hint: Free translation; check with tutor. Mr Wong replies: 呢个人真唔客气勒！我走勒！ni1 go3 jan4 zan1 m4 haak3 hei3 laak3! ngo5 zau2 laak3! (This person is really impolite! I'm leaving!)

items.prompt: f. FS: Oh, he's gone!
items.answer: keoi5 zau2 zo2 laak3!

exercises.title: Practice 2
exercises.instructions: Show your disagreement with the following negative statements by providing the affirmative counterparts. Example: nei5 mou5 si4 gaan1 you have no time —> ngo5 jau5 si4 gaan1 aa3 I do have time (the particle aa3 serves to soften the force of the disagreement)

items.prompt: sik6 hoi2 sin1 m4 gwai3 (Eating seafood is not expensive)
items.answer: sik6 hoi2 sin1 hou2 gwai3 aa3

items.prompt: di1 haau2 si3 tai4 muk6 m4 hai6 hou2 naan4 (The exam questions are not very hard)

notes.title: It's electric
notes.body:
In this unit we have met the word din6 jing2 for movie film. It literally means electric shadows and was an ingenious way of coping with the new concept when it first burst on to the Chinese scene. The word din6 electric was itself originally borrowed from the word meaning lightning and it has been put to very good use ever since. We met electric heater din6 nyun5 lou4 in Unit 8.
Din6 ce1 (lit.) electric vehicle: tram
Din6 waa2 (lit.) electric speech: telephone
Din6 si6 (lit.) electric vision: television
Din6 nou5 (lit.) electric brain: computer

notes.title: A problem of age
notes.body:
When someone gives his age he will give it in seoi3 not in nin4. Well, that's easy enough. What is sometimes a problem is sorting out what seoi3 means, because traditionally Chinese people were born one seoi3 old and then added another seoi3 to their age at each Chinese New Year.
So a Chinese born on the last day of the lunar year would already be loeng5 seoi3 old the next day, while a Western baby born on the same day would not even have got to 'one' yet!
